title: Protecting Children Online: What the Online Safety Act Has—and Hasn't—Delivered
label: 13 October 2026 · Online Safety Act: children
summary: Witnesses from the Molly Rose Foundation, Internet Matters and LSE told the committee that harms to children online have grown since the Online Safety Act (OSA) passed, and that the regulator Ofcom has been slow and cautious in enforcing the law. New risks—group-based grooming ("com groups"), AI chatbots, AI-generated sexual images and cross-platform harms—are not well covered by the current, content-focused regime. Witnesses called for stronger, outcome-focused duties on platforms (an overarching duty of care), removal of safe-harbour limits, better age assurance, proactive technology with privacy safeguards, clearer enforcement powers (including interim takedowns and criminal measures) and a national push on media literacy and reporting routes for children.

glossary.definition: UK law intended to make online services safer, especially for children, by requiring platforms to manage risky content and design.
The UK communications regulator charged with enforcing parts of the Online Safety Act.
A legal protection that limits how far a regulator can require platforms to go beyond certain compliance steps.
Methods platforms use to check users' ages so they can apply age-appropriate measures.

Automated systems that suggest content to users, which can amplify harmful material.
Tools (like hash-matching or classifiers) that automatically detect and block harmful content before users see it.

chapters.title: How risks have changed since the Act
chapters.takeaway: Experts say harms to children have grown and become more complex—new threats overlap with old ones and the OSA has not yet reduced exposure.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To start: how have risks to children online changed since the Online Safety Act?

turns.speaker: Andy Burrows
turns.text: Risks have got worse and more complex. We see ‘com groups’—organised, sadistic groups grooming children across platforms, leading to sexual abuse, live-streamed suicide and other extreme harms.

turns.speaker: Andy Burrows
turns.text: These groups are hybrid threats: they don't fit neatly into sexual abuse, suicide or terrorism boxes, which makes them hard for the Act to tackle.

turns.speaker: Professor Sonia Livingstone
turns.text: Research categorises risks as content, contact, conduct and commercial. All have increased; exposure to self-harm, violent and sexual content and bullying has doubled in some European surveys over five years.

turns.speaker: Professor Sonia Livingstone
turns.text: Ofcom's own stats show no change in children's exposure before and after the Act, so benefits aren't yet visible.

turns.speaker: Katie Freeman-Tayler
turns.text: New technologies matter too: AI chatbots are conversational, are being used for advice or emotional support, and many children trust them—around a quarter used them for advice and 40% trusted the advice in recent UK research.

turns.speaker: Katie Freeman-Tayler
turns.text: AI-generated sexual images are rising: earlier estimates suggested ~500,000 UK children had encountered a nude deepfake; IWF data shows AI CSAM increases and more use in sextortion.

chapters.title: Where the Act and Ofcom are falling short
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses say the Act is too siloed and Ofcom has been slow, cautious and constrained by safe-harbour rules and evidential hurdles.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Which risks is the current framework least equipped to address?

turns.speaker: Katie Freeman-Tayler
turns.text: The Act focuses on harmful content, but many harms come from platform design—recommender systems, notifications and features that keep children online longer.

turns.speaker: Professor Sonia Livingstone
turns.text: Personalised feeds are weaponised against vulnerable children; it's hard for researchers or parents to see what an individual child receives.

turns.speaker: Andy Burrows
turns.text: Ofcom has been asleep to com groups. There were international warnings from the FBI and others in 2024, but Ofcom was slow to update its risk register and act.

turns.speaker: Lord Storey
turns.text: Are online services making changes after the Act?

turns.speaker: Professor Sonia Livingstone
turns.text: Some platforms added user guidance, parental tools and age checks early on, but safety-by-design steps have tailed off.

turns.speaker: Katie Freeman-Tayler
turns.text: Families see more reporting tools and age checks, but many children say age checks are easy to bypass; a third had circumvented one in our study.

turns.speaker: Andy Burrows
turns.text: Our research found no material drop in teens seeing suicide/self-harm content: 48% of girls saw such content, down only one point since before the Act. Algorithms drive much of this exposure.

chapters.title: Enforcement gaps and a high-harm forum example
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom lacks powers or has used them slowly: witnesses want broader scope, interim takedowns, criminal sanctions and action even when services try to geo-block.

turns.speaker: Baroness Owen of Alderley Edge
turns.text: Tell us about Ofcom's limits in enforcing against a US-based suicide forum.

turns.speaker: Andy Burrows
turns.text: That forum reportedly contributed to 160+ deaths. It has been allowed to operate in plain sight. Ofcom took too long to act and avoided powers the Lords had sought to give it for small high-harm sites.

turns.speaker: Andy Burrows
turns.text: Three specific gaps: jurisdiction issues when sites geo-block, no clear power for interim service disruption while investigating imminent risk, and weak use of criminal sanctions against operators.

turns.speaker: Professor Sonia Livingstone
turns.text: That slow investigation has retraumatised bereaved families; it shows the system isn't set up to act quickly on clear, dangerous harms.

turns.speaker: Baroness Elliott of Whitburn Bay
turns.text: Is Ofcom 'learning to walk before it runs' fair?

turns.speaker: Andy Burrows
turns.text: No. Ofcom has been risk averse and too slow against big tech. The EU's Digital Services Act enforcement was quicker and had more impact because firms took notice.

chapters.title: Technology fixes, safe harbour and age bans
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses back proactive tools and stronger duties, oppose safe-harbour protections, worry about an under-16 social media ban unless age assurance and other effects are solved.

turns.speaker: Lord Tarassenko
turns.text: Should Ofcom be able to require proactive technology like automated classifiers and hash-matching?

turns.speaker: Professor Sonia Livingstone
turns.text: Proactive tech could help but raises privacy risks and needs independent scrutiny; platforms are black boxes and we lack data to check effectiveness.

turns.speaker: Andy Burrows
turns.text: Proactive tech is essential to stop harmful content before it's spread. But if the Act keeps acting as a floor and lawyers chip away at measures, the tools won't be used effectively.

turns.speaker: Katie Freeman-Tayler
turns.text: We support proactive tech if it's effective and privacy-preserving. But safety needs a layered approach—one tool won't solve recommender problems or design harms alone.

turns.speaker: Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate
turns.text: What about safe harbour—should it go?

turns.speaker: Andy Burrows
turns.text: Yes. Safe-harbour provisions are limiting. They keep obligations low and lock in the status quo, so remove them or rework them so platforms must do more.

turns.speaker: Professor Sonia Livingstone
turns.text: Safe harbour was meant as a first step; instead it's become a ceiling. The EU's DSA doesn't offer the same protection and is pushing safety-by-design harder.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: On under-16 social media bans—will they work?

turns.speaker: Andy Burrows
turns.text: A ban risks creating a false sense of safety unless age assurance works and platforms keep protections. Australia's experience shows many children still access platforms.

turns.speaker: Katie Freeman-Tayler
turns.text: A ban could reduce harms if age assurance is robust. But harms will likely shift to other services—messaging, gaming, AI chatbots—so the OSA must keep covering all platforms.

turns.speaker: Professor Sonia Livingstone
turns.text: Children want community and information online. Bans must avoid removing their rights and should be weighed against realistic, privacy-respecting age checks and safer design.

chapters.title: Top recommendations
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses’ near-term priorities: make platforms subject to an outcome-based duty of care, remove safe-harbour limits, improve age assurance, give Ofcom stronger rapid powers, require reporting routes and boost media literacy.

turns.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town
turns.text: If you had to give two top priorities for the committee's recommendations, what would they be?

turns.speaker: Professor Sonia Livingstone
turns.text: First, make age assurance effective and privacy-respecting so we know who is a child online. Second, create reliable reporting and remedy routes that children can use and trust.

turns.speaker: Katie Freeman-Tayler
turns.text: First, treat media literacy as a national priority—support teachers and parents so children get the skills to navigate risks. Second, focus on outcomes, not compliance: what do we want children's online lives to look like?

turns.speaker: Andy Burrows
turns.text: I want a third-Session Bill to fix the Act: restore an overarching duty of care with clear outcomes, remove safe harbour, strengthen incentives (including criminal sanctions) and learn from financial-services enforcement on conduct.

turns.speaker: Baroness Caine of Kentish Town
turns.text: How should a regulator handle hybrid, cross-platform harms?

turns.speaker: Andy Burrows
turns.text: Make co-operation mandatory: platforms must share signals, risk assessments and work together on proactive measures. Embed co‑operation in duties at each stage—assessment, mitigation and monitoring.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Any final words?

turns.speaker: Professor Sonia Livingstone
turns.text: We need clearer, stronger rules about features and design, joined up internationally, and systems that let researchers and the public see what platforms actually do.

turns.speaker: Katie Freeman-Tayler
turns.text: Regulation, technology and education must work together. Pressure on platforms should be sustained so compliance delivers real safety for kids, not just paperwork.

turns.speaker: Andy Burrows
turns.text: This is preventable harm. Fix the incentives, beef up enforcement powers, and protect children now—otherwise tragedies like Molly's will keep happening.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all for your expertise and the work you do protecting children online.
